cases.basis: Calendar arithmetic and three accounting identities that hold for any price path: money in is the schedule count times the contribution; portfolio value is cash plus the market value of the holdings; and a full rebalance, which is defined as buying the underweight and selling the overweight until the targets are met, leaves the portfolio at its targets on the bar it runs. Fees are charged at 0.1% so they can move the restored weights only in the fourth significant figure. A holding of negative units or a negative cash balance would mean the engine sold something it did not own or spent money it did not have.

cases.basis: The trigger is a function of day D's close: 'the highest close in the lookback window of bars before that day' compared with today's close. The comparison cannot be made until day D's close exists, so no order placed on it can be filled at that same close - neither the purchase nor, when the reserve is a holding, the sale of the reserve asset that pays for it. Executing both legs at the signal bar's close buys and sells at prices that were only knowable after the decision, which flatters every figure the tool reports and cannot be reproduced by anyone following the rule. The lookback of 20 bars and the threshold of 5% are chosen so that a ten-year 15%-volatility path produces many firings, giving the count something to count. TESTCASES P1 records that this build is not expected to satisfy it.

expect.why: If the trigger never fired the case would prove nothing.

The first executable bar after a close-based signal is the next bar.

The same rule when the reserve is a holding rather than cash.
The same rule.
Funding the purchase means selling the reserve asset; that sale is part of the same decision and is priced on the same information, so it cannot be filled at the signal bar's close either.
Stated as a minimum over every funding sale, so one exempt sale is enough to fail.

cases.basis: The asset is deterministic: zero volatility and -20% a year, so its close falls by the same factor every bar and the highest close of any window that ends before today is always the oldest close in that window. Over L bars the fall is 1 - 0.8^(L/B), where B is the number of bars a year. For any plausible B between 150 and 400 that is between 1.2% and 2.2% over 20 bars and between 3.6% and 6.4% over 60 bars, so a 3% threshold cannot fire on a 20-bar anchor and must fire on a 60-bar one. A 20-bar setting that fires anyway is reaching further back than it claims (an all-time high, or the untrimmed series); a 60-bar setting that never fires is not reaching back at all. The nesting statement is the same fact stated generally: a longer window has a maximum at least as high, so its condition is satisfied on a superset of days. Finally, the anchor must use bars strictly before today: an anchor that includes today's own close would let the rule fire one bar earlier than the causal definition allows.

expect.why: A 3% threshold against the highest close of the previous 20 bars, on a path that loses at most 2.2% over 20 bars, can never be satisfied.
With nothing ever deployed and a 0% risk-free rate, the portfolio is exactly the money paid in: 120 monthly top-ups of 1,000.
The same money, still in the reserve.
Over 60 bars the same path falls at least 3.6%, which clears the 3% threshold, so the reserve must be deployed.
max over 60 bars >= max over 20 bars at every date, so the 60-bar condition holds on a superset of the days the 20-bar condition holds on.

The first deploy cannot precede the first bar at which the causal condition is true. Zero is same-bar execution, one is next-bar execution; a negative value means the anchor window was allowed to include the deploy bar's own close, which is the look-ahead this case is here to exclude.
Well-formed inputs.

cases.basis: The Date Range tooltip states the rule: 'The simulation runs over the dates every asset has in common ... Each ticker is trimmed to that shared set of trading days, so the portfolio is only valued on days where every asset has a price.' NYSE and ASX keep different holiday calendars and sit on different sides of the date line, so their common dates are a strict subset of either one's, and the two-asset run therefore has fewer bars than the single-asset run over the same requested window. That is correct behaviour, but it changes the sample the user's comparison is drawn from, so it has to be visible in the result rather than only in a tooltip. TESTCASES P3 records the shrinkage as silent in this build, so the notice check is the one expected to fail.

expect.why: The axis the tooltip promises is exactly the intersection: no date where an asset has no price, and no date dropped that both assets have.

cases.basis: Ranking the assets needs each one's trailing return, and a trailing return that ends at day D's close is only known once day D has closed. Splitting that same day's contribution by that ranking, at that same day's closing prices, spends information the buyer did not have. The causal ranking is the one ending at the previous close. Three synthetic assets with different drifts and volatilities reorder often enough over ten years that the two rankings disagree on many top-ups, and those disagreements are the only ones that carry information: on them, the realised split must follow the causal ordering. TESTCASES P4 records this build as ranking same-bar.

expect.why: 120 whole months in the window.
Without disagreements the test is vacuous; three assets with 25%, 12% and 4% volatility reorder many times over 120 monthly observations.

Stated positively: on every top-up where the two rankings disagree, the realised split must be the causal one.
Rank weights of 50/30/20 sum to 100, so the whole contribution is deployed and none is lost in the ranking step.
Well-formed inputs.

cases.basis: A portfolio of one asset held at 100%, with Constant Allocation splitting each contribution by the weights and buying, with no fees and with idle cash earning nothing, is the same model as plain dollar-cost averaging into that asset: the same money arrives on the same dates and buys the same asset at the same closes. The two tools share the synthetic-asset generator and the same seed, so the price path is the same input in both. Two renderings of one model must therefore agree to the last cent; any difference is one of the two being wrong, and the user has no way to tell which.

cases.basis: The Target Weights tooltip states the contract the user is held to: 'The weights must add up to 100%.' A set that does not is therefore an input error, and there are only two honest responses: refuse to run, or normalise and say so - 60 and 50 become 54.5455% and 45.4545%. Silently treating 60 and 50 as shares of 110 without saying so, or as shares of 100 with the remaining 10% invented, both put a portfolio on screen that the user did not ask for. A weight of zero is a legitimate instruction to hold none of an asset, so no unit of it may ever be bought. A rank tail of zero is the same instruction expressed by rank. A negative weight is a short position, which this model has no representation for, so the realised share of that asset cannot be below zero and no holding or cash balance may go negative. None of these depends on the price path.

cases.basis: The Reserve tooltip offers two kinds of waiting room: 'Risk-Free Account: the money is held as cash and earns the risk-free yield. An asset: the money is parked in that holding and follows its price until it is deployed.' Each of the four states puts that promise under a condition the form allows the user to create, and the assertions are the same in all of them because they are the accounting rules the model cannot break whatever the prices do: a reserve cannot be sold below empty, cash cannot go negative, every contribution is still accounted for, a reserve that has been deleted has to fall back to something rather than leave the engine pointing at an asset that no longer exists, and a trigger firing against an empty reserve deploys nothing rather than borrowing. A threshold of 0.1% against the previous five bars fires on most bars, which is what drains the reserve and produces the empty-on-fire condition repeatedly.

cases.basis: Two independent claims. First, rebalancing frequency and trading cost: for a portfolio whose weights drift as a random walk, the trade needed to restore the targets grows with the square root of the time since the last rebalance, so total turnover over a fixed horizon scales with the number of rebalances divided by that square root - it rises as rebalancing gets more frequent. Rebalancing at every one of 120 monthly top-ups must therefore trade more in total than rebalancing on 40 quarter dates, and at a flat 0.1% per trade more turnover is strictly more cost. Second, parked cash: a trigger that needs a 99% fall from the month's open cannot fire on a 15%-volatility path, so every contribution stays in the Risk-Free Account for the rest of the run and the ending value is the contributions compounded at the stated yield and nothing else. At 0% that is exactly the money paid in; at 5% it is the sum over the 120 contribution dates of 1000*(1.05)^t, where t is the years from that date to 2024-12-31, which is 154,704.22 under annual compounding, 155,720.78 if the yield is applied continuously and 155,746.78 if it is applied as 5%/365 daily. Simple, non-compounded interest would give 150,021.36 and no interest at all 120,000, so the check separates 'earns the risk-free rate' from both of the ways of not doing so.

cases.basis: A buying fee of 0.1% has only two sensible readings: the fee comes off the contribution before it buys, so units*price is 0.999 of the money, or the fee is added on top of the trade, so units*price is 1/1.001 = 0.999001 of it. Both land within a millionth of 0.001, so the implied fraction identifies the fee rate without needing to know which convention the engine uses, and it is scale-free, so it does not depend on the price path. Whatever the page reports as fees must be that same money - a fee figure that does not reconcile with the gap between money in and money invested is decoration. A 100% fee is the degenerate end of the same arithmetic: it is a reachable input, it can legitimately buy nothing, and what it may not do is produce NaN, negative units, negative cash or a value larger than the money paid in.

cases.basis: Every figure here comes from the calendar alone. A fortnight is fourteen days, not half a month: counting from Sunday 2015-01-04 to Saturday 2024-12-28, a span of 3,647 days, gives 261 fourteen-day steps, whereas a schedule that fired twice a month would give 240 - the two cannot be mistaken for each other. A quarterly schedule offset to the second month of each quarter fires in February, May, August and November; offset to the third it fires in March, June, September and December; either way that is four times in each of ten years. A yearly schedule on 15 January in a window that opens on 1 February 2015 misses 2015 and fires nine times, from 2016 to 2024. Day 31 has to be clamped to the end of a shorter month: February must still receive its contribution, which after nearest-trading-day snapping lands no earlier than the 26th, and it must not leak into March, which would leave February empty and March doubled. A yearly schedule on 15 January inside a window that opens on 1 February 2015 and closes that December never fires at all, which is an empty result to be reported, not a crash and not a NaN.

cases.basis: The Simulation Seed tooltip states the contract: 'Fixes the random numbers behind simulated assets, so the same seed always reproduces the same Geometric Brownian Motion price path.' A path that depends on anything other than the seed, the parameters and the window - which portfolio is looking at it, which rebalancing method that portfolio uses, which of the two tools is drawing it, how many times the page has been run, or the machine's timezone - is not reproducible, and every comparison the tool exists to make becomes a comparison of two different assets. The last check is the converse and guards against a seed that is ignored: a different seed must give a different path, otherwise 'fixes the random numbers' is vacuously satisfied by a constant.
